blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: For most languages, automatic speech recognition (ASR) is limited less by model architecture than by a lack of accurately transcribed spontaneous speech. We present Monsoon, a framework for collecting such data at scale. It elicits unscripted conversations between paired contributors, screens recordings with automated classifiers, corrects transcripts over five levels of human review, and selects segments for lexical and acoustic coverage. It has collected speech in 50 languages; we analyse seven 3,500-hour corpora. At equal volume, its quality stages reduce semantic word error rate (WER) by 10-39% relative to a conventional protocol. Compared with an architecture-matched baseline trained on public corpora, Whisper fine-tuned on Monsoon performs comparably on the baseline's own test sets and reduces semantic WER by 20-44 points on conversational benchmarks. The gains transfer to a second architecture and grow with data volume. We release the framework, its quality-control models, and the fine-tuned models.
blocks.zh: 对于大多数语言来说,自动语音识别(ASR)受到模型架构的限制较少,而缺乏准确的转录自发语音. 我们提出 " 蒙松 " ,这是大规模收集此类数据的框架。 它引来配对贡献者之间的无标本对话,用自动分级器来显示录音,在人文审查的5个层次上校正笔录,并选择分块进行词汇和声学覆盖. 它收集了50种语言的演讲;我们分析了7个3500小时的蝎子. 在等量时,其质量级比常规协议将语义词出错率(WER)降低10-39%. 相较于在公共公司训练的建筑相配基线,Whisper在"蒙松"上的微调在基线本身的测试集上可以比较性地表现,在对话基准上将语义WER减少20-44分. 收益转移到了第二个架构,随着数据量的增长而增长. 我们发布框架, 其质量控制模型, 和微调模型。

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
For English, where transcribed speech is abundant, the best ASR systems now average below 6% word error rate (WER) across
the Open ASR Leaderboard [ 20 ] . Across languages,
accuracy tracks the quantity of such data; for Whisper, WER decreases
log-linearly with the hours of training audio per language, halving with every
sixteen-fold increase [ 17 ] . For most languages, accuracy
is therefore largely limited by the amount of suitable training data rather
than by model architecture. Existing corpora for these languages are small,
dominated by read or prompted speech that is mismatched to spontaneous usage,
or weakly verified: annotation guidelines vary within and between corpora,
crowd-sourced transcripts are rarely checked, and inconsistent orthography
fragments the label space [ 21 ] . Much of this noise is
unsystematic, so text normalisation cannot fully correct it.

blocks.en:
Efforts to scale speech data have mostly favoured volume over control.
Crowd-sourced read speech [ 2 ] , parliamentary and
religious recordings [ 22 , 15 ] , and weakly supervised web
audio [ 17 ] give broad language coverage, but the source
fixes their domain, speaking style, and label quality. Models trained on large
aggregations of such data do well on test sets drawn from the same collections
and lose much of their accuracy on conversational
speech [ 6 , 4 ] . What is
scarce, then, is not speech data in general but data collected and verified for
the conditions a deployed model faces.

blocks.en:
We propose Monsoon , a framework that enforces data quality at scale
through automated filtering and human verification. The framework has been
used to collect speech in 50 languages. Here we analyse seven of them,
including Kashmiri, which has no public training corpus of comparable size,
each with about 3,500 hours of transcribed spontaneous speech in
single-speaker segments taken from the separately recorded channels of
two-party conversations. Per language, these corpora exceed publicly
available corpora [ 12 , 1 ] in transcribed
volume and, on average, in speaker coverage. Whisper
medium [ 17 ] fine-tuned
on Monsoon matches the architecture-matched IndicWhisper [ 6 ] on
the latter’s own test sets and outperforms it by 20 to 44 points of semantic
WER on independently collected spontaneous speech. At equal volume
and with the same elicitation, the framework’s quality stages reduce error by
10 to 39% relative over a conventional protocol. The gains transfer to
SraVaani-1.0 [ 16 ] , an independently pretrained, Indic-specialised
FastConformer model; the fine-tuned Whisper model
outperforms all but one of five commercial systems; and error is still falling
at the full collected volume. A 10-hour sample of each of the 50 languages is
available on request.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Conversational speech corpora. Transcribed spontaneous
speech has long been expensive to collect. Switchboard [ 10 ] established telephone
conversation as a training resource for English, and the Babel
programme [ 9 ] extended it to low-resource languages at tens
of hours per language. IndicVoices [ 12 , 1 ] collects extempore and conversational speech across 22 languages, with 11.2K
transcribed hours in total. Benchmarks of accented and in-the-wild speech
continue to find that existing systems perform poorly outside read
speech [ 13 , 4 ] .

sources that already exist: volunteer read speech [ 2 ] ,
parliamentary recordings [ 22 ] , religious texts [ 15 ] ,
weakly supervised web audio [ 17 ] , or aggregations of
earlier public corpora [ 6 ] . The source fixes their speaking
style and domain, and label quality is controlled, if at all, by filtering
after the fact.

blocks.en:
Data quality in ASR training. Orthographic complexity
predicts ASR error across languages [ 21 ] , speaker count
at fixed volume drives robustness to unseen accents [ 23 ] ,
and non-intrusive predictors such as DNSMOS [ 18 ] measure
acoustic quality at corpus scale. These factors have been studied in isolation,
not combined in a collection process and tested against conventional
collection at equal volume.

blocks.en: 3 The Monsoon Framework
blocks.zh: 3 蒙松框架

blocks.en:
Contributors. Monsoon recruits speakers per language from an
existing contributor network, including rural and semi-urban regions, and
admits only those who pass a proficiency screen in the target language.
Contributors are paid, give informed consent, and grant rights for model
training and distribution. A per-language cap on recorded speech keeps any
speaker below 0.2% of a corpus.
blocks.zh:
供养者. 蒙松语从一种语言中招募演讲者
现有捐助网络,包括农村和半城市地区,以及
只接纳那些通过目标语言熟练度屏幕的人.
向捐款者支付费用,给予知情同意,并授予模式权利
培训和传播。 记录的语音的每个语言封顶都保留着任何
演讲者低于尸体的0.2%。

blocks.en:
Elicitation. The platform pairs two contributors, typically
strangers, and records their conversation peer-to-peer on their own phones,
one speaker per channel. Each session follows a topic: a one-sentence scenario
with five sub-topics revealed in turn, sustaining 10 to 20 minutes of unscripted
speech. Topics are generated by Gemini 3.7 Flash across 35 everyday domains,
conditioned on the topics already accepted in each. Sub-topics follow one of
six conversational arcs, and constraints require every stage to involve both
speakers, at least one stage to elicit numbers and one a procedure, and at
least two to require naming real places, shops, or products, while the prompt
itself stays region-neutral and excludes role-play. Candidates are embedded
with BGE-small and rejected if their cosine similarity to
the nearest accepted topic exceeds 0.8, a threshold tuned by inspecting
near-duplicate pairs; the rejection rate rises from 16% to
over 50% as a domain saturates. Accepted topics are translated and revised by
native speakers. The pool holds about 5,000 topics per language and grows
with recording, so no pair receives the same topic twice.

blocks.en:
Gating and segmentation. Classifiers fine-tuned from XLS-R
300M [ 3 ] on over 20,000 hours of labelled audio verify
language and speaker gender with over 95% held-out accuracy, and
PANNs [ 14 ] rejects recordings in which any recorded-media
class, such as music, exceeds probability 0.5. Each channel is segmented
separately with WebRTC VAD at pauses of at least 2 s, with a
soft limit of 15 s, so every segment has one speaker. Segments with DNSMOS
P.808 [ 18 ] below 2.6, between “poor” and “fair” on the
absolute category rating scale, are kept only if human reviewers judge them
intelligible, and a per-language Whisper medium
model [ 17 ] , fine-tuned on 1,000 hours of annotated
data, produces draft transcripts.

blocks.en:
Transcription. Drafts pass five levels, each an edit by one
annotator verified by another: the first corrects the draft against the
audio, and later levels target ambiguous pronunciations, code-switch
boundaries, named entities, and spelling variants. Numbers are written as words, and segments still disputed after the
fifth level are re-transcribed. Annotators are audited automatically on
batches of 100 segments and flagged for manual review if a batch contains
out-of-script characters, repeats the same insertion across many segments, or
systematically raises the minimum CER against several open-source ASR outputs;
the thresholds are adjusted per language as annotator behaviour is observed. After all
validation steps, an in-house team audits a sample of each annotator’s
segments, and that annotator’s segments enter the corpus only if at least 98% of the
sampled segments are judged correct.

blocks.en:
Experimental setup. We fine-tune Whisper
medium [ 17 ] separately on each Monsoon corpus, and

five epochs of AdamW at a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , 500 warm-up steps, and

decay 10 − 3 10^{-3} and its default SpecAugment. We evaluate on the Vistaar test
sets [ 6 ] , CommonVoice [ 2 ] ,
FLEURS [ 7 ] , GramVaani, IndicTTS, Kathbath and its noisy
variant [ 11 ] , and MUCS [ 8 ] , which are in
distribution for the IndicWhisper baseline but not for Monsoon; and on
IndicVoices [ 12 ] and Voice of
India [ 4 ] , which are out of
distribution for both. We report semantic WER, in which an LLM judge
(Gemini 3.6 Flash) discounts differences that preserve the spoken
content [ 19 ] ;
Voice of India is scored with its orthography-aware
variant [ 5 ] . Kashmiri is excluded from the comparisons,
since none of the baseline or commercial systems supports it.

trained on about 10,700 hours of public corpora drawn from the same sources
as the Vistaar test sets. With the architecture held fixed, the comparison
mainly reflects the training data, although the two training recipes differ. Fig. 1 reports both
models per language.

On the Vistaar sets, which favour IndicWhisper because its training data
shares their sources, the two polygons largely coincide

within one point in Hindi, Marathi, and Bengali; only in Tamil does

test sets’ own sources without having seen any of them.

blocks.en: 4.2 What does the pipeline itself contribute?
blocks.zh: 4.2 (中文(简体) ). 管道本身有何贡献?

blocks.en:
Figure 2: Semantic WER (%) at 1,000 hours: conventional protocol (grey)
vs. Monsoon (blue), same recipe. Labels: relative reduction.

报告  Mon(蓝),食谱相同. 标签:相对减少.

blocks.en:
To isolate the pipeline, we compare against data from the same elicitation
process, with the same topics, pairing, and devices, but processed under a
conventional protocol: recordings are checked only for spoken language and
receive a single level of human transcription instead of five, with no further
gating, quality review, or selection. Both are Whisper medium
trained on 1,000 hours with the same recipe, so they differ only in how the
data was gated, transcribed, and selected. The
Monsoon model is better on both benchmarks in Hindi, Tamil, and Telugu
(Fig. 2 ), reducing error by 10 to 39% relative. The reduction appears on both IndicVoices
and the Vistaar sets, so it is not confined to spontaneous speech. Because elicitation is identical on
both sides, the difference cannot be attributed to topics, pairing, or
recording conditions. The gain
is largest in Telugu, at close to 40% on both benchmarks, indicating that at
equal volume the gating, verification, and selection stages together account
for much of the accuracy of the resulting models.

blocks.en: 4.3 Do the gains transfer across architectures?
blocks.zh: 4.3 (中文(简体) ). 收益会跨建筑转移吗?

blocks.en:
To test whether the gains depend on Whisper, we continually fine-tune
SraVaani-1.0 [ 16 ] , which differs from Whisper in encoder
architecture, decoder formulation, and pretraining data, and is already
specialised to Indian languages. Continual fine-tuning on Monsoon reduces its
semantic WER on IndicVoices by 13 to 28% relative across four representative
languages, Hindi, Bengali, Gujarati, and Telugu, with the largest gain in
Gujarati. On Hindi, where we evaluate the full suite, read-speech
benchmarks such as FLEURS and Kathbath show only marginal increases, of at
most 0.4 points, a regression that standard replay of the original training
data is designed to mitigate. The gains are therefore not specific to one
architecture, and they add accuracy on top of a model already trained on large
in-language data.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We presented Monsoon, a framework for collecting spontaneous speech for ASR
training at scale, and used it to build corpora of about 3,500 hours in each
of seven languages. At equal volume and with the same elicitation, its gating,
verification, and selection stages reduce error by 10 to 39% relative over a
conventional protocol. Models trained on Monsoon match a read-speech baseline
on its own test sets and outperform it by 20 to 44 points on independently
collected spontaneous speech, the gains transfer to a second, Indic-specialised
architecture, and accuracy is still improving at the full collected volume.
A 10-hour sample of each of the 50 languages is available on request. Future work will extend the framework to further
languages.
